To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
SkinnerDB is an efficient, reliable, and robust query execution strategy that is able to outperform state of the art query execution strategies on a wide variety of benchmarks.
(1) SkinnerDB reliably finds the best join order for every query, (2) SkinnerDB does so with minimal overhead, and (3) SkinnerDB outperforms all baselines, including adaptive methods.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of reliable join ordering, i.e. the problem of finding the best join order given the query, the data, and the query optimizer's knowledge of both.
a new quality criterion and a corresponding new query evaluation algorithm for reliable join ordering.
the following aspects: 1) A new quality criterion for join order optimization.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

SkinnerDB is the first system that reliably finds the optimal join order for any query, and that it does so at a cost comparable to the performance of a database system that does not try to find the optimal join order.
SkinnerDB is the first query execution engine that can consistently outperform adaptive query execution methods.
SkinnerDB is the most promising approach towards reliable join order optimization.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

SkinnerDB is a new, reliable query evaluation method for relational databases that is competitive in performance, and that it provides a new quality criterion that can guide the design of future query processing methods.
SkinnerDB is a new query processing engine that uses reinforcement learning to optimize join orders.
SkinnerDB can reliably execute queries with a small fraction of the cost of existing systems.
The main takeaway from our work is that
reliable join ordering is possible and practical, even for very large queries.
the performance of a query optimizer can be significantly improved by optimizing for a more appropriate criterion, in this case, the expected cost of a query relative to an optimal join order.
the performance of query execution strategies can be improved by using the execution history to guide the execution of future queries.
